name: Inner Circle
tagline: An invite-and-vetting based dating app that sells paid membership tiers on top of a curated member pool.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The software here is a swipe deck, a chat thread, and a photo uploader, all of which an agent can produce before lunch. The product is not the software, it is the several thousand screened single people in your city who opened the app this week. A dating app with one user is a photo album, and a dating app with twelve users is a group chat with extra steps. You also inherit the parts nobody wants to build: abuse reporting, photo moderation, age and identity checks, payment handling, and the App Store review process for all of it. Build the client if you want to learn; you cannot build the pool.
coreLoopDIY: A local, invite-only intro board for a friend group where two people only see each other's interest when it is mutual.
requirements: A machine or cheap VPS to host it
Everyone you want on it has to actually sign up, which is the whole problem
whatYouLose: The member pool, which is the entire product
Vetting and screening, so your version is whoever you can nag into joining
Moderation, blocking, and reporting tooling for when someone behaves badly
Mobile apps and push notifications, so nobody checks it twice
Identity and age verification, plus the legal exposure of running a dating service without it
moatNotes: Dating is a two-sided market with brutal local density requirements: liquidity in Amsterdam does nothing for a user in Leeds, so the moat is rebuilt city by city and is hard to copy for exactly that reason.
whyPeopleStillPay: People pay for access to strangers who are already there, already screened, and already in the mood to meet someone. No amount of clean code substitutes for that, and the paid tier mostly buys visibility and filtering inside a pool you did not have to assemble. The vetting story, whether or not it holds up in practice, is also a brand promise: users are paying to believe the other profiles are less of a lottery. None of that is a feature you can ship.
notes: The app is a weekend; the city full of vetted singles is not. The moat is two-sided local liquidity plus a curation promise, rebuilt market by market.
prompt:
Build a self-hosted, invite-only "mutual intro board" for a small private group. This is not a dating app clone, it is the honest consolation: a place where a closed circle of people can privately flag interest in meeting each other, and nobody learns anything unless the interest is mutual.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Next.js (App Router) with TypeScript and Tailwind
- SQLite via better-sqlite3, file at ./data/circle.db
- Sessions via signed httpOnly cookie, secret in .env as SESSION_SECRET
- No external services, no analytics, no email provider, no payment code

In scope:
- Invite codes only: an admin CLI script `npm run invite` prints a single-use code. There is no public signup.
- Signup with code: display name, one-line bio, up to three photos stored on local disk under ./data/uploads, served through an authenticated route only.
- Member directory: profiles visible only to signed-in members.
- Interest: on another member's profile, a single "interested" toggle. Store it privately. Nothing is shown to the other person.
- Mutual reveal: when A and B are both interested, create a match row and show it on a /matches page for both, with a plain text thread between the two of them.
- Block: blocking hides both profiles from each other, kills any existing match, and prevents new interest.
- Admin page listing members with a remove button that deletes their account, photos, interests, and threads.

Out of scope, do not build:
- Swipe UI, algorithmic ranking, geolocation, push notifications, payments, identity or age verification, native apps

Details:
- Seed script that creates an admin account from ADMIN_EMAIL and ADMIN_PASSWORD in .env
- Write .env.example, never commit .env, add ./data to .gitignore
- Store nothing in a third-party service; the whole thing must run with `npm run dev` on one machine
- README with: how to invite, how to back up (copy ./data), and a blunt line saying this works for a group of about ten people who already know each other and does not work for strangers
